summary: Extends the Access Network Identifier option for Proxy Mobile IPv6, introduced in RFC 6757. That option lets a Mobile Access Gateway tell the mobility anchor about the access network. This specification adds more kinds of identifying information.

plainLanguage.summary: A note that says which door a visitor came through now carries a few more details.

questions: what is the pmipv6 ani option
what is the ani update timer
what is the mag group identifier
subtitle: Three new sub-options let a Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateway report civic location, a group ID and how often to refresh.

tldr.problem: The Access Network Identifier option from RFC 6757 could carry geographic coordinates, but in indoor Wi-Fi deployments those are hard to get, and the anchor had no way to control how often it hears about changes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7563 adds a Civic-Location sub-option (type 4), a MAG-Group-Identifier sub-option (type 5) and an ANI Update-Timer sub-option (type 6) that the MAG and the LMA negotiate.
tldr.outcome: A Mobile Access Gateway can now describe where a client is by street or room address and by AP group, and the Local Mobility Anchor can throttle how often it receives updates. The RFC updates RFC 6757.

today: RFC 7563 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2015. It updates RFC 6757, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Extend the ANI Option
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6, a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) tells a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) about the access network a client is using. RFC 6757 defined the Access Network Identifier (ANI) option for this, with Network-Identifier, Geo-Location and Operator-Identifier sub-options. The LMA may use the data to pick policies such as Quality of Service or Deep Packet Inspection, and may share it with location-based applications.

This RFC adds three things aimed at WLAN deployments. Indoor access points are hard to place with geospatial coordinates, while a civic location is often enough. Operators group APs into AP-Groups, and a group identifier can stand in for coarse location, such as a floor, or serve as a common policy for all APs in the group. Finally, when the MAG sits with a wireless LAN controller, roaming between APs is hidden from the LMA, so the data goes stale unless something controls refreshing.
sections.plainLanguage: A note about where you are used to list only map coordinates, which are hard to work out indoors. Now it can also say the street address and which group of access points you are using.

sections.title: The Civic-Location Sub-Option
sections.content:
The Civic-Location sub-option has ANI Type 4. It carries the civic location of the mobile node as known to the MAG. Civic location means a civic address, such as a street address or a room within a building, as opposed to longitude, latitude and altitude.

The header holds an ANI Type, an ANI Length (the length in octets excluding the type and length fields), a Format byte and a Reserved byte, followed by the location. Only Format 0 (Binary Encoding) is defined; 1 through 255 are reserved. It reuses the civic address encoding of RFC 4776, leaving out the first 3 octets, so the field starts with a two-letter ISO 3166 country code such as US, followed by one or more civic address elements.

Reserved MUST be zero when sending and is ignored on receipt. The civic location length SHALL NOT exceed 253 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a slot for a postal-style address, like a country plus a street or a room number. It cannot be longer than a set size.

sections.title: The MAG-Group-Identifier Sub-Option
sections.content:
The MAG-Group-Identifier sub-option has ANI Type 5 and identifies the group affiliation of the MAG within its Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain. The identifier is a 3-octet unsigned integer assigned to a group of MAGs.

It is not assumed to be globally unique across operators, though it should be unique within one operator network. In domains spanning several operators, the RFC recommends adding the Operator-Identifier sub-option from RFC 6757 to ensure uniqueness. A MAG configured with a group identifier should send it in the Proxy Binding Update (PBU). How the identifier is configured is out of scope, and how the LMA uses it is left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a team number for a bunch of access points. The number only has to be different from other teams run by the same company.

sections.title: The ANI Update-Timer and Its Negotiation
sections.content:
The ANI Update-Timer sub-option has ANI Type 6 and a 16-bit unsigned Update-Timer value. Its unit is 4 seconds, which matches the time units of the binding lifetime. A value of 0 means the MAG sends an updated ANI as soon as it sees a change. A non-zero value means the MAG may wait and send updates when the timer expires.

The value is negotiated. A timer in a PBU is a proposal, and the LMA may change it in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA). If the LMA's value differs, the MAG should use the LMA's value. If the PBA has no Update-Timer, the MAG behaves as in RFC 6757. The LMA can echo, raise or lower the value; for example, it can raise it to get fewer updates or set 0 to hear of changes right away.

The introduction gives an example of a stadium Wi-Fi deployment where the LMA does not want updates more often than 100 seconds and proposes 100 seconds as the value.
sections.plainLanguage: The anchor can say how often it wants a fresh note. Zero means tell me right away, and a bigger number means wait that many four-second ticks.

sections.title: MAG and LMA Behavior
sections.content:
Both sides extend their state. The MAG's Binding Update List entry and the LMA's Binding Cache entry (from RFC 5213) each gain three parameters: civic location, MAG group identifier and ANI Update-Timer.

A configured MAG includes the ANI option with its sub-options in all PBUs, including lifetime extension and deregistration. When ANI parameters change, the MAG checks whether the Update-Timer has expired. If it has, the MAG sends a PBU with the ANI option; if not, it does not. When the timer expires, the MAG sends a PBU only if the parameters changed since the last report. The MAG may send a PBU early, for example to start a QoS request (see RFC 7222), and then it must reset the Update-Timer.

The LMA must process the ANI option in a PBU. An LMA that does not understand the option skips it. A PBU without the ANI option removes the stored access network information from the session. An LMA that supports the sub-options echoes the ones it accepted in the PBA, should not alter the Civic-Location and MAG-Group-Identifier values, and may change the Update-Timer. If a MAG gets a successful PBA without the option, it may log the event and, by local policy, even end the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway only sends a new note if something changed and enough time has passed. The anchor writes back which parts it understood, and may change the waiting time.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated three type values from the registry "Access Network Information (ANI) Sub-Option Type Values": 4 for the Civic-Location sub-option, 5 for the MAG-Group-Identifier sub-option and 6 for the ANI Update-Timer sub-option. Each can be carried in the Access Network Identifier mobility option.
sections.plainLanguage: The three new kinds of note were each given an official number so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The sub-options travel in PBU and PBA messages like any other ANI sub-option, so they inherit the guidance of RFC 5213 and RFC 6757. The RFC adds that the civic location is considered very sensitive, so the signaling must be secured. RFC 5213 specifies IPsec, and operators can potentially apply IPsec ESP with confidentiality and integrity protection.

Another way to protect users is not to send the location. Users of the Civic-Location sub-option should provision values with the highest possible level of granularity, such as province or city rather than a specific address. Information the MAG learns over DHCP or other protocols could be compromised without proper security, causing wrong policy enforcement at the LMA. The RFC suggests securing the path between the MAG and the access points with IPsec, TLS or other security protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Where someone is can be private. So the note should be sent in a locked envelope, and it is best to give only a rough place like a city.

items.label: Civic-Location

fields.name: ANI Length
fields.desc: Length excluding the type and length fields; always 2.

fields.desc: Unsigned integer in units of 4 seconds; 0 means update as soon as a change is seen.
